subject: history
note: Original class-wise notes following the NCERT 6–12 history sequence used in UPSC/BPSC. Not a copy of the textbooks.

chapters.title: What, Where, How and When?
chapters.summary: History is recovered from manuscripts, inscriptions, archaeology and oral memory. People lived along the Ganga, Narmada, Indus and in the hills and plateaus. Dates are approximate; BCE/CE is the modern convention. Always ask: whose past is being told?

chapters.title: From Hunting-Gathering to Growing Food
chapters.summary: Foragers used stone tools and moved with seasons. Farming and herding (Mehrgarh and other sites) meant surplus, pottery, houses and new inequalities. Domestication of plants and animals is the real revolution.
points: Gender and labour in early farms
chapters.exam: Link to agriculture beginnings in GS-I.

chapters.title: In the Earliest Cities
chapters.summary: Harappan cities (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi) show planning, drainage, craft and long-distance trade. The script is undeciphered. Decline involves climate, rivers and economic stress—not a single simple invasion story.

chapters.title: What Books and Burials Tell Us
chapters.summary: The Rigveda is a window into early Vedic life: cattle, clans, gods of nature. Megalithic burials in the Deccan and south show iron, horses and status in death. Texts and graves together reconstruct social worlds.

chapters.title: Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic
chapters.summary: Mahajanapadas (c. 6th century BCE) include kingdoms and ganasanghas like Vajji. Magadha rises on iron, forests, rivers and ambitious rulers. The varna order and taxes on peasants fund armies.

chapters.title: New Questions and Ideas
chapters.summary: Urbanism and inequality spark the Upanishads, Buddhism and Jainism. The Buddha teaches dukkha and the middle path; Mahavira stresses ahimsa and ascetic rigour. Sanghas become new social spaces.

chapters.title: Ashoka, The Emperor Who Gave Up War
chapters.summary: The Mauryas unify a huge territory. After Kalinga, Ashoka broadcasts dhamma through edicts: non-violence, welfare, respect for sects. The state still taxes and rules; dhamma is moral policy, not the end of empire.

chapters.title: Vital Villages, Thriving Towns
chapters.summary: Iron tools expand plough agriculture. Land grants, crafts, punch-marked coins and Northern Black Polished Ware mark towns such as Pataliputra, Mathura and coastal ports. Village and city depend on each other.

chapters.title: Traders, Kings and Pilgrims
chapters.summary: The Silk Routes, maritime trade, the Kushanas and Satavahanas, and Chinese pilgrims (Faxian, Xuanzang) show India in a wider world. Bhakti to Shiva–Vishnu and the spread of Buddhism travel with merchants.

chapters.title: New Empires and Kingdoms
chapters.summary: Guptas, Vakatakas, Pallavas, Chalukyas and Harsha use land grants, samantas and courtly Sanskrit. Assemblies in the south (sabha, ur) matter. Genealogy and prashastis are political advertisements.

chapters.title: Buildings, Paintings and Books
chapters.summary: Stupas, temples (from rock-cut to structural), Ajanta paintings, the epics, Puranas and Tamil Sangam poetry are sources of belief and power. Art is never only decoration.

chapters.title: Tracing Changes through a Thousand Years
chapters.summary: 700–1750 CE sees new technologies, groups (Rajputs, Marathas), Persian-influenced administration and shifting religious vocabularies. Historians use chronicles, inscriptions and architecture. ‘Hindu’ and ‘Muslim’ are not frozen blocs.

chapters.title: New Kings and Kingdoms
chapters.summary: Regional dynasties (Cholas, Palas, Rashtrakutas, Gurjara-Pratiharas) live on land grants, temple-centred economies and warfare. Chola navy, local assemblies and bronze sculpture are high-yield.

chapters.title: The Delhi Sultans
chapters.summary: From the Mamluks to the Lodis, the Sultanate experiments with iqta, token currency (Muhammad Tughluq), market control (Alauddin Khalji) and a mixed elite. Architecture from Qutb to Tughlaq is a source.

chapters.title: The Mughal Empire
chapters.summary: Babur to Aurangzeb: mansab, jagir, zabt, sulh-i-kul under Akbar, expansion and later crisis. Court chronicles (Akbarnama) and paintings document power. Succession and jagir shortage weaken the later empire.

chapters.title: Rulers and Buildings
chapters.summary: Mosques, tombs, temples and gardens announce piety and sovereignty. Qutb, Vijayanagara, Fatehpur Sikri, Taj Mahal—read plan, material and inscription, not just beauty.

chapters.title: Towns, Traders and Craftspersons
chapters.summary: Temple towns, port towns (Surat, Masulipatnam) and craft centres thrive. Hundi, guilds, and European companies enter Indian Ocean trade. Urban decline in some 18th-century towns is political.

chapters.title: Tribes, Nomads and Settled Communities
chapters.summary: Gonds, Ahoms, Banjaras and shifting cultivators sit outside neat varna maps. States try to tax and settle them; some found kingdoms. Ahom state-building in Assam is a classic case.

chapters.title: Devotional Paths to the Divine
chapters.summary: Bhakti and Sufi movements speak in regional languages: Kabir, Nanak, Mirabai, Chaitanya, Nayanars–Alvars, Chishti saints. They question ritual monopoly without always overthrowing caste.

chapters.title: The Making of Regional Cultures
chapters.summary: Kathak, miniature painting, Malayalam, Bengali, Jagannath cult, martial traditions—regions craft identities through court, temple and language. Kerala’s mahabharata recensions and Bengal’s temples are examples.

chapters.title: Eighteenth-Century Political Formations
chapters.summary: Mughal decline opens space for Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad, Marathas, Sikhs, Jats and Mysore. Successor states still use Mughal forms. This is the eve of colonial conquest.

chapters.title: How, When and Where
chapters.summary: Colonial archives, surveys and maps created a dated, official India. Periodisation (Hindu–Muslim–British) is a colonial habit; historians now stress processes. Dates still matter if you know why they were chosen.

chapters.title: From Trade to Territory
chapters.summary: The East India Company becomes a territorial power after Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764), Diwani of Bengal, Subsidiary Alliance and Doctrine of Lapse. War, diplomacy and revenue—not just trade—explain the Raj.

chapters.title: Ruling the Countryside
chapters.summary: Permanent Settlement (Bengal), Ryotwari and Mahalwari reshape agrarian relations. Indigo, opium and cotton tie peasants to world markets. Famine and indebtedness follow extraction.

chapters.title: Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age
chapters.summary: Forest laws, moneylenders and missionaries disrupt Adivasi life. Birsa Munda and other movements imagine a just past. Colonial ‘civilising’ meets resistance.

chapters.title: When People Rebel — 1857
chapters.summary: Sepoy grievances, annexations, greased cartridges and popular support in Awadh and Bihar (Kunwar Singh) make 1857 a widespread revolt. It fails militarily but ends Company rule.

chapters.title: Civilising the ‘Native’, Educating the Nation
chapters.summary: Orientalists vs Anglicists (Macaulay), Wood’s Despatch, and nationalist education (Tagore, Mahatma Gandhi) debate what knowledge is for. English creates a new middle class and a political public.

chapters.title: Women, Caste and Reform
chapters.summary: Sati debates, widow remarriage, girls’ schooling, Phule, Ambedkar, Periyar, Narayana Guru—reform is contested. Women are subjects, not only symbols. Caste critique is central to modern India.

chapters.title: The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947
chapters.summary: From associations to Congress, Moderates–Extremists, Swadeshi, Home Rule, Gandhi’s satyagrahas, mass movements, revolutionaries, and the road to 1947. Include peasants, workers, women and depressed classes.

chapters.title: India After Independence
chapters.summary: Constitution, linguistic states, planning, non-alignment, and the challenge of equality. Integration of princely states and nation-building continue the freedom story.

books.book: India and the Contemporary World — I

chapters.title: The French Revolution
chapters.summary: 1789 attacks privilege: Estates, Bastille, Declaration of Rights, republic, Terror, Napoleon. Ideas of liberty–equality–fraternity travel globally, including to Indian political thought.

chapters.title: Socialism in Europe and the Russian Revolution
chapters.summary: Industrial inequality breeds socialist thought. 1917 topples Tsarism; Bolsheviks take power, civil war, and a planned state. The idea of workers’ revolution shapes the 20th century.

chapters.title: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
chapters.summary: Versailles, Depression and propaganda enable Hitler. Racism, war and the Holocaust are the core of Nazi rule—not only dictatorship. Democracy’s collapse is a warning.

chapters.title: Forest Society and Colonialism
chapters.summary: Scientific forestry, reserved forests and timber for empire criminalise customary use. Rebellions (Bastar, Java) show ecological and social conflict.

chapters.title: Pastoralists in the Modern World
chapters.summary: Colonial borders, waste-land rules and taxes squeeze Raikas, Bakarwals, Maasai. Mobility is not ‘backwardness’; it is an economy. Climate and the state still squeeze pastoralists.

chapters.title: Peasants and Farmers
chapters.summary: Enclosures in England, American wheat expansion, opium in India—capitalism remakes the countryside. Indian peasants enter a world market on unequal terms.

books.book: India and the Contemporary World — II

chapters.title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
chapters.summary: Nations are made through language, war and revolution: 1789, 1848, Bismarck’s Germany, Italian unification. Nationalism is both liberation and exclusion.

chapters.title: Nationalism in India
chapters.summary: From Rowlatt and Jallianwala to Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India; the Congress, Muslims, Dalits and business have different hopes. 1947 is freedom and partition together.

chapters.title: The Making of a Global World
chapters.summary: Silk routes to colonial globalisation: corn, cotton, indenture, world wars and Bretton Woods. India is in the story as colony and as migrant labour.

chapters.title: The Age of Industrialisation
chapters.summary: Britain’s factories, India’s deindustrialisation, mills in Bombay–Ahmedabad, and the myth that industrialisation is only steam. Handicrafts survive and adapt.

chapters.title: Print Culture and the Modern World
chapters.summary: Printing creates public opinion: Reformation, newspapers, novels, Indian presses, and colonial censorship. Print is a political technology.

chapters.title: From the Beginning of Time
chapters.summary: Hominin evolution, stone tools, language and the spread of Homo sapiens. Prehistory is archaeological, not textual.

chapters.title: Writing and City Life
chapters.summary: Mesopotamia: cities, cuneiform, temples, trade and law. Urbanism needs writing and surplus.

chapters.title: An Empire Across Three Continents
chapters.summary: Rome: army, slavery, law, citizenship, Christianity, and eventual transformation. Empire is logistics and ideology.

chapters.title: The Central Islamic Lands
chapters.summary: From the Prophet to caliphates: ummah, sharia, Abbasid urban culture, Crusades and Mongols. Islam as civilisation, not only conquest.

chapters.title: Nomadic Empires
chapters.summary: The Mongols under Genghis Khan connect Eurasia: terror, trade protection, and a vast steppe state. Nomads are political innovators.

chapters.title: The Three Orders
chapters.summary: Medieval Europe: clergy, nobility, peasantry; feudal ties, manors, and the Church. Crisis of the 14th century (plague, war) remakes society.

chapters.title: Changing Cultural Traditions
chapters.summary: Renaissance humanism, print, new science, Reformation. Europe’s ‘modernity’ is cultural before it is industrial.

chapters.title: Confrontation of Cultures
chapters.summary: 1492 onwards: Spain–Portugal, gold, disease, and the destruction of indigenous American worlds. Encounter is conquest.

chapters.title: The Industrial Revolution
chapters.summary: Britain’s coal, cotton, steam, urban misery and the idea of progress. Industry is energy + labour + empire markets.

chapters.title: Displacing Indigenous Peoples
chapters.summary: Settler colonies in the Americas and Australia: land grabs, missions, and surviving native politics. Compare with India’s tribal story carefully—contexts differ.

chapters.title: Paths to Modernisation
chapters.summary: China, Japan and (comparatively) the West take different roads: Meiji, revolutions, and anti-imperial nationalism. Modernity is plural.

books.book: Themes in Indian History — I, II, III

chapters.title: Bricks, Beads and Bones (Harappan)
chapters.summary: Mature Harappan urbanism, craft, weights, decline. Archaeology over speculation. Dholavira’s water systems and craft villages (Lothal dock debate) are map points.

chapters.title: Kings, Farmers and Towns
chapters.summary: Mahajanapadas to Mauryas: inscriptions (Ashoka), coins, towns. The political economy of early historic India.

chapters.title: Kinship, Caste and Class
chapters.summary: Mahabharata as a source for kin, gotra, varna and gender. Social history uses texts critically, not as photographs.

chapters.title: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings
chapters.summary: Sutta, stupa, sculpture: Buddhism’s architecture and the Sanchi case. Patronage and meaning of monuments.

chapters.title: Through the Eyes of Travellers
chapters.summary: Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta, Bernier: foreign observers with biases. Use them as sources, not as the last word.

chapters.title: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
chapters.summary: Devotional Islam and Hindu paths, Kabir’s radical speech, Guru Nanak’s panth. Overlap and conflict both exist.

chapters.title: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
chapters.summary: Hampi’s sacred and royal landscape, Rayas, nayakas, water and temples. Archaeology + Raya chronicles + foreign visitors.

chapters.title: Peasants, Zamindars and the State
chapters.summary: Ain-i-Akbari as source: village, zamindar, zabt. Agrarian society funds the Mughal empire.

chapters.title: Kings and Chronicles
chapters.summary: Mughal court culture, manuscripts, paintings, the making of official history (Akbarnama). Power writes its own story.

chapters.title: Colonialism and the Countryside
chapters.summary: Bengal zamindars, the Permanent Settlement, the Company Raj in the village, and the Deccan riots. Revenue is the colonial state’s spine.

chapters.title: Rebels and the Raj
chapters.summary: 1857 as event and as later nationalist memory. Visuals, proclamations and repression. Bihar and Awadh remain essential.

chapters.title: Colonial Cities
chapters.summary: Presidency towns, hill stations, segregation, municipal government, and Indian neighbourhoods. The city is a colonial project and an Indian one.

chapters.title: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement
chapters.summary: Gandhi’s politics as mass communication: salt, khadi, satyagraha, and limits (Dalit question, 1947). Read sources: letters, newspapers, rumours.

chapters.title: Understanding Partition
chapters.summary: 1947 as history and trauma: politics of the 1940s, violence, refugees, memory. Not only ‘two-nation’ as destiny.

chapters.title: Framing the Constitution
chapters.summary: Constituent Assembly debates: rights, federalism, language, separate electorates. The Constitution as a historical document of 1946–49.
